history.origins: Dates back to at least the early 1700s in France. It was a popular parlor game among the bourgeoisie before being overshadowed by BÃ©zique and Belote.
timeline: 1710s: First descriptions of Minette appear in gaming manuals.
1800s: Remains a niche but respected game in regional France.
Present: Rarely played, mostly of interest to historical card game researchers.
20th Century: Documented by historians like David Parlett as a precursor to modern French partnership games.
history.cultural: Reflects the formal, turn-based social play of the French Enlightenment.
history.evolution: The game's 'Exchange' mechanic (discarding and drawing) served as a blueprint for the more famous Ã‰cartÃ©.

setup.players: Two players only. Minette is played exclusively by two players; each is dealt twelve cards and the remaining eight cards form the talon (stock), from which trump is determined. There are no partnerships.
setup.dealing: Each player is dealt 12 cards. The remaining 8 cards form a 'Talon' (Stock).

rules.objective: Score 60 points through winning tricks and declarations.
rules.gameplay: Standard trick taking. Must follow suit. If you can't follow, you MUST trump. Higher card of the led suit or higher trump wins the trick.
keyRules: Must follow suit when possible; if void in led suit, must trump.
Higher card of led suit wins unless trumped; higher trump wins the trick.
Score 60 points through tricks and declarations (marriage) to win.

strategy.basic: Keep track of the Aces. In a 32-card deck, Aces are nearly impossible to beat unless someone trumps. If you have the lead, play your Aces early to secure point-tricks before the opponent can void a suit.
strategy.intermediate: Trump Management: Use the exchange (if allowed in your variant) to build a 'Long Suit'. If you can control the trump suit with 4-5 cards, you can dominate the end-game and capture the opponent's high-value side cards.
strategy.advanced: The 'Seven Swap': If you have the 7 of trumps, don't swap it too early. Wait until the opponent leads a high trump, then swap and play the new trump to seize the lead. This defensive move can break their momentum.
tips: Memory: Since 12 cards are dealt to each, and 8 are in the talon, you initially know 12/32 cards. Pay attention to the trump card!
Focus on the 'Last Trick' (10 bonus points) as it often determines the winner in a close 60-point match.

scoring.description: Kings, Queens, and Jacks carry 1-3 points. Aces are worth 11 points. The last trick adds a bonus.
